02 The big picture

Think of an experienced dock supervisor

Someone who's worked the same floor long enough that they don't need a checklist to notice something's off — a forklift moving oddly, a door open at the wrong time, an aisle emptier or busier than usual. They just know, because they know what a normal shift looks like. Observer is trying to give a camera that same kind of instinct, for one specific site.

Learns from experience

Not from a manual or a rulebook — from watching the site itself.

Notices what's different

Compares what it sees right now against what it's come to expect.

Specific to its own floor

What's "normal" at one site isn't assumed to be normal everywhere.

03 Under the hood — the pipeline

Five steps, a bit more detail than the summary deck

Watch

Reads the live video, frame by frame, from whichever camera it's pointed at.

→

See & track

Finds people/vehicles in each frame and follows them — so it knows this is the same forklift as a second ago.

→

Describe the scene

Turns everything visible into a set of numbers for that moment: how many, how spread out, how fast.

→

Learn a baseline

Collects many of those "status snapshots" while things are normal, and finds the pattern.

→

Compare & decide

Every new snapshot is checked against that pattern. Far enough off = alarm, with a saved image.

04 The modes it runs in

It's always in exactly one clear mode

Idle

Camera preview only. Not judging anything yet. This is what it boots into.

Collecting baseline

Gathering "normal" snapshots — the learning phase.

Training

A short pause while it turns what it collected into a baseline.

Monitoring

Comparing live activity against that baseline, continuously.

Alarm

Something didn't match — flagged, with a snapshot as evidence.

Error

Something broke, e.g. the camera disconnected. A safe fallback.

Good line for the meeting: "Stop always brings it back to Idle, from any mode — including Error. Nothing gets permanently stuck."

05 What you'll actually click through

The live dashboard — the one you'll show Stefan

  • Top: the live camera view, exactly what the system sees.
  • Status: whichever mode it's in, from the previous slide.
  • Progress bar: appears while Collecting Baseline is running.
  • Alert list: recent flagged moments, each with its own snapshot.
  • Controls: one Start/Stop button, and a camera picker — only changeable while Idle.
06 Why no manual training

Nobody hand-labels "suspicious" footage

It's closer to training a new hire by having them watch the floor for a while, rather than handing them a rulebook that tries to list every possible bad scenario in advance.

No dataset to build

No one collects or labels example footage before it can start.

Adapts per site

The baseline is specific to whatever this camera normally sees.

Re-learns on the fly

Move the camera, or start a fresh scan, and it learns that new normal.

07 Why it's built in swappable pieces

Like modular warehouse racking, not poured concrete

Every part — the camera, the vision model, the decision model, the alert channel, the dashboard — is a separate, swappable module. You can change one without rebuilding the rest of the structure.

  • Swap the camera type — a different brand, or existing CCTV.
  • Swap the alert channel — SMS, email, or an existing security system.
  • Add a new way to view it later — not locked into today's web dashboard.
08 Being honest about where it stands

Say this part out loud, comfortably

Working today

  • Live detection & tracking loop
  • Automatic baseline learning
  • Real-time alerts with snapshots
  • Live web dashboard with start/stop control

Still in progress

  • Saving a learned baseline so it survives a restart
  • More alert integrations
  • Other client apps beyond the web dashboard

This honesty is a strength, not a weakness — it shows the core idea already works, and invites Stefan into shaping what's next, rather than reacting to a locked-down finished product.

09 Questions Stefan might ask — technology

Have these ready

Q."Isn't this just motion detection?"
No — motion detection asks "did something move." Observer looks at the whole scene: how many objects, how fast, and whether they're grouping or scattering.
Q."Does it need the internet or a cloud service?"
No — it runs on-site, on its own small computer. Video doesn't need to leave the premises.
Q."Can it recognize faces or read license plates?"
No — it doesn't identify who or what something is. It looks at movement patterns and flags what's unusual, not identity.
Q."What about bad weather or changing light?"
A fair concern, and honestly one of the things worth testing in a pilot — the baseline is learned from this camera's typical conditions.
10 Questions Stefan might ask — practical

And these

Q."Is this a finished product we could buy today?"
No — it's a working prototype. A solid foundation for a pilot, not an off-the-shelf product yet.
Q."What would a pilot actually look like?"
Pick one site, install a camera and a small on-site computer, let it learn for a period, then review together what it flagged.
Q."What does it cost?"
Not priced yet — this stage is about proving the idea on a real site, not selling a finished product. Better to say that plainly than guess a number.
11 Before you walk in

A few do's and don'ts

Do

  • Lead with the problem it solves, not the technology.
  • Be upfront that it's a working prototype.
  • Treat Stefan's tough questions as a good sign, not a threat.
  • Suggest a small pilot as the natural next step.

Don't

  • Promise a delivery date.
  • Quote a price.
  • Claim it recognizes faces, plates, or identities.
  • Claim it's already validated on his exact cameras and site.
12 Quick glossary

If a term comes up

Baseline

The pattern of "normal" activity the system learns for one specific site.

Anomaly detection

Flagging what doesn't match the baseline, instead of matching against a list of known bad events.

Edge device

A small computer at the site itself (rather than a server elsewhere) doing the processing.

Pilot

A small, time-boxed test at one real site to see how it performs before any wider rollout.

13 Your cheat sheet

If you remember nothing else, remember this

"Observer is a camera system that learns what normal looks like at a specific site, and flags the moments that don't match — running on cheap, on-site hardware, with no cloud required."

Three strengths

  • Learns automatically — no manual setup per site.
  • Understands relationships, not just motion.
  • Runs locally — data stays on-site.

One honest caveat, and the ask

  • It's a working prototype, not a finished product.
  • The ask: "Would you be open to a small pilot at one site?"

You know this well enough now.
